journal_sources.method: Crossref journal cursors and publisher Harvest publication dates fetched separately on 2026-11-20. The comparison counts all CC BY records with an abstract, as in September. It also counts publisher-typed articles or letters within that group. Registry intake requires an exact original date and a then-effective version-of-record license. The previous filter discarded every outgoing update.
journal_sources.denominators: The 222 CC BY records with abstracts comprise 219 articles or letters, two comments and one reply. The six original articles with a registered self-correction include only one with an eligible license. The eligible article appeared on September 17 and was corrected on October 15. Retrospective collection uses the latest registered text and correction history.

previous_english_corrections.old_headline: Simulated quantum reservoirs trace memory to Liouvillian modes, dissipation and feedback
previous_english_corrections.old_summary: Five theory/simulation preprints ask how relaxation, dissipation and delayed feedback generate memory and nonlinearity in quantum reservoirs; none report experiments.
previous_english_corrections.old_synthesis: All five preprints are theoretical or numerical studies asking which physical dynamics of open quantum reservoirs produce task-relevant memory and nonlinear processing, and they give different answers. In driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs, arxiv:2609.20345 finds enhanced memory near both first-order and continuous dissipative transitions. Its exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition attributes capacity mainly to finite-rate modes and their cross-terms, with weak contribution from the gap mode. arxiv:2609.23429 proposes a Volterra-weight factorization W^(q)=BH^(q) separating input-history pathways from readout visibility, and argues that weak measurement and delayed feedback can activate otherwise invisible covariance modes. arxiv:2609.27072 proposes coherent waveguide-QED feedback to a Kerr resonator. In NARMA-n tasks, the optimal delay approximately tracks the input-product lag. In neutral-atom simulations, arxiv:2609.28441 finds controlled dissipation necessary for the echo-state property and reports Mackey-Glass solutions with N=5 atoms. arxiv:2609.22791 models a Gaussian cavity-magnomechanical reservoir with strong memory, limited nonlinearity, and a measurement-budget-dependent optimal encoding.
previous_english_corrections.new_headline: Models trace quantum reservoir memory to Liouvillian modes, dissipation and feedback
previous_english_corrections.new_summary: Theory and simulation preprints tie reservoir memory to model-specific causes: Liouvillian modes, evolution time, dissipation, coherent delayed feedback.
previous_english_corrections.new_synthesis: These theoretical and numerical preprints ask which mechanisms and control parameters set memory and nonlinear processing in quantum reservoirs. None reports an experimental measurement, and the answers differ by model. For driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs, arXiv:2609.20345 finds enhanced memory and nonlinear processing near both first-order and continuous dissipative transitions. Its Liouvillian-mode decomposition attributes the gain mainly to finite-rate modes rather than the gap mode. arXiv:2609.23429 develops a Volterra-weight framework, W^(q)=BH^(q), and argues that thermalization shifts the response toward the most recent input. In that framework, weak measurement and delayed feedback can activate or return information. In a proposed waveguide-QED reservoir with a Kerr resonator, arXiv:2609.27072 reports that the optimal feedback delay approximately tracks the NARMA-n input-product lag. In a Gaussian cavity magnomechanical proposal, arXiv:2609.22791 finds that evolution time controls the balance between memory and nonlinear processing. In simulated neutral-atom arrays, arXiv:2609.28441 reports that controlled dissipation is necessary for fading memory and that performance peaks at the edge of quantum chaos.

interpretation.newly_ranked: The three dark energy studies estimate constant or evolving equation-of-state parameters using two supernova analyses and gravitational lensing. The binary studies evaluate photometric, astrometric and spectroscopic companion detection. The English copy distinguishes simulated accuracy, recall and companions ruled out. The three denominators support no common efficiency estimate.
interpretation.still_missing: The review separated the stellar benchmark catalogue from two pipelines and separated one rotation-period catalogue from two cluster studies. It split direct detection on full KiDS images from two crop-based lens searches. None of the intended three-paper sets ranked.
interpretation.retained_or_changed: Thirteen of twenty coherent September groups kept their exact membership. Four others gained a study, including one CMS tracking group and three groups interpreting the LZ recoil. The coupling and recoil-suppression groups lost one or more members. No paper from the former diffusion group ranked. The intact October false merge combines optical delay, broadband-phase and quantum Fisher information studies. No member of the fifteen previously justified exclusions appeared in a new rank.

synthesis.membership: Five original papers plus one study of self-interacting dark matter.
synthesis.assessment: The new text distinguishes which theoretical interpretations check relic abundance, solar capture and elastic scattering. The old universal constraint claim is absent.

synthesis.membership: Three of the four original papers.
synthesis.assessment: The shorter group no longer includes the conformally coupled study that reported a lower minimum chi-squared. The text gives the reported model comparison for each remaining study. Removing the fourth paper makes this a different comparison.

The synthesis softened the original claim to “activate or return information” but still left the intervention-to-outcome mapping ambiguous. Weak measurement exposes covariance modes. Delayed feedback creates return pathways for earlier inputs.

interpretation.decision: The prespecified requirement for an independent test passed. Two of five omissions ranked, and intact mixed controls fell from two to one. This authorized the August trials only.

single_change_journal_recollection.method: The hosted rerank collected the same September dates at the corrected journal intake commit, using the prior result-review method and existing model receipts.

independent_weeks.protocol: For each previously reserved seven-day period, read the five highest and up to five other lowest ranks, then five source-stratified excluded sets across both review stages. Compare each English headline, short summary and synthesis with the cited work. A ranking passes only with supported selection and copy before annotations. Each stratum requires nine passes in ten cases.
independent_weeks.editorial_scope: One reader assessed the rank- and source-stratified cases. A dated English correction preserves the original score. August 12 supplied four distinct low-ranked cases after selecting its five highest.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Do the papers produce explicit binary CSS qLDPC/bicycle/Tanner-type codes at finite length with reported [[n,k,d]] parameters (rate and distance)?
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Group-lifted qLDPC searches report explicit codes; Tanner distances are only upper bounds
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Preprints report explicit finite [[n,k,d]] qLDPC codes; quantum Tanner distances for n in [500,1000] are randomized upper bounds, not certified values.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All four preprints search algebraic lifts or group constructions for explicit finite-length qLDPC codes with stated [[n,k,d]], but the distances carry different certainty. arXiv:2608.09115 certifies distances exactly via the F4 additive-code correspondence for cyclic bicycle codes. Its [[66,20,7]] code reaches kd²/n=14.85, compared with 12 for [[144,12,12]]. arXiv:2608.08996 uses a multi-agent search restricted to binary CSS codes with n≤400 and weight w≤10. It reports [[288,16,18]] at w=7 and [[234,28,18]] at w=10, and lists a [[336,12,≤24]] code only as a candidate. Its failure rates come from BP-OSD decoding under code-capacity depolarizing noise. arXiv:2608.12509 gives quantum Tanner distances only as upper bounds from up to 350 million sQetch trials. arXiv:2608.07431 targets neutral-atom AOD hardware. Its self-dual [[132,30,12]] code has a simulated logical error rate of 1.0(+0.9/−0.6)×10⁻⁹ per round per qubit, assuming a physical error rate of 10⁻³.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All four studies construct finite quantum error-correcting codes and report their length, logical dimension and distance information. The brief identifies exact distances, search upper bounds and simulated logical error separately.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Dissipation engineering that stabilizes or enhances persistent ergotropy and energy storage in open quantum batteries
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Theory models use engineered dissipation to stabilize ergotropy in open quantum batteries
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Theory preprints model how restricted decay, reservoirs, collective dissipation or a catalyst mode can sustain extractable energy in open quantum batteries.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All four preprints are theoretical. Each treats dissipation as a resource for retaining ergotropy rather than only as a loss channel, and none reports an experimental measurement. In a Λ-configuration atomic-ensemble model, arXiv:2608.06479 finds that quantum jumps become constructive when decay is restricted to excited→metastable transitions and ground-state decay is fully suppressed. Under that condition, the battery reaches full charge and all stored energy is extractable. arXiv:2608.08619 couples a driver to a hot reservoir and a cache to a cold reservoir, which yields a population-inverted steady state with finite ergotropy. For uniformly spaced multilevel batteries, stored energy and ergotropy scale approximately linearly with the number of levels. In a transverse-field Ising model, arXiv:2608.09693 shows that collective dissipation produces dark states, counted by the Catalan sequence for even sizes, and frozen states. Any ergotropy or power advantage depends on temperature, magnetic phase and system size. Using Lindblad simulations, arXiv:2608.10032 finds that an off-resonant catalytic mode suppresses backflow and that steady-state ergotropy increases with battery size N_B.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: Each model computes energy extractable from an open battery. The brief gives the different decay, reservoir and catalyst conditions and the temperature dependence of the collective effect.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Constraints on whether late-time dark energy deviates from a cosmological constant/ΛCDM using SNIa and background expansion data
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Model-dependent SNIa and expansion fits give only marginal hints of non-Λ dark energy
unannotated_english_cases.summary: New SNIa-based fits: binned w(z) marginally dynamical in the first bin; fractional HDE not AIC/BIC-preferred; HL q(z) fit reads quintessence-like.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: Three preprints test whether late-time dark energy departs from Λ using SNIa together with other background-expansion data. Each answer depends on the adopted model. arXiv:2608.08007 fits a piecewise-constant w_iCDM model in 7 redshift bins to Planck 2018 TT/TE/EE/lensing, DESI DR2 BAO and Pantheon+ data. It uses implicit likelihood inference (SNLE, 6 rounds of 20000 CLASS simulations). The first bin marginally favors dynamical dark energy, the other constrained bins are consistent with Λ at 68% C.L., and w_5 and w_6 are unconstrained. arXiv:2608.09379 fits three fractional holographic dark energy cutoffs (Hubble, future-event and particle horizons) to SN+OHD+DESI DR2 data. All three give a marginally lower χ²_min than ΛCDM, but AIC and BIC show no significant preference. Adding CMB distance priors strongly disfavors FHDEH and FHDEP. arXiv:2608.10242 fits a logarithmic q(z) parametrization within Hořava–Lifshitz gravity to cosmic chronometer and Pantheon+SHOES data. It finds q_0<0 and t_0≈13.7 Gyr. Within this parametrization, Om(z) slopes indicate quintessence-like w>−1.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All three compare a late-time expansion fit with a cosmological-constant description. The brief preserves the redshift-bin uncertainty, the information-criterion result and the conditional interpretation of the kinematic diagnostic.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Silicon photonic multiplexed links managing inter-channel crosstalk, with transmission quality demonstrated (crosstalk suppression and BER/capacity)
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Silicon photonic chips suppress mode and polarization crosstalk in multiplexed fiber links
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Three preprints report on-chip crosstalk handling: BER <1e-4 with 4 ms updates, <-11.1 dB supermode crosstalk at 1.2 Tbit/s, and a >1.8 Tbit/λ/s engine.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three preprints experimentally address inter-channel crosstalk in space- or mode-division multiplexed links using silicon photonic hardware. The approaches and reported metrics differ. arxiv:2608.06986 pairs a silicon photonic processor with an FPGA running training-free blind source separation. It shows photonic separation of signals up to 100 GBaud and continuous adaptation for two 64 GBaud channels over few-mode fiber, keeping BER below 10^-4 under dynamic crosstalk with a 4 ms per-update control latency. arxiv:2608.11099 suppresses crosstalk passively, using a hierarchical second-order discrete supersymmetric transformation for six-supermode multiplexing on SOI and silicon nitride. Its devices show <2.6 dB insertion loss and <-11.1 dB crosstalk over a 100-nm range, and the silicon device carries 1.2 Tbit/s aggregate with all channels below the 7% HD-FEC threshold. arxiv:2608.11639 reports a monolithic engine exceeding 1.8 Tbit/s/λ that self-configures for two, four or six spatial and polarization channels while mitigating dynamic crosstalk. The authors claim >5,000-fold power and latency reductions relative to state-of-the-art DSP at MIMO order six.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All three experiments test inter-channel crosstalk in multiplexed optical links. The brief assigns the bit-error rate, insertion loss, throughput and adaptation latency to their respective devices.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Resource and complexity scaling of quantum PDE solvers with grid size or dimension
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Quantum PDE solver scaling: regularity bounds, conditional high-dimension advantage
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Preprints bound quantum PDE costs via Gevrey regularity, claim advantage in high dimension under oracle assumptions, and find FDTD condition numbers saturate.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: Three preprints ask how quantum PDE solver resources scale with grid size, precision or dimension, and give different answers. arXiv:2608.07893 links Gevrey regularity of periodic functions to the qubits needed for high-precision Fourier amplitude encoding. It derives resource bounds, including precision-dependent cutoffs and gate costs, for linear PDEs with periodic or Dirichlet boundaries, the latter via thin Gevrey collars, and applies them to Poisson equations. The abstract does not quantify the curse-of-dimensionality claim in its title. arXiv:2608.09675 lifts nonlinear scalar conservation laws to a Liouville equation, applies Schrödingerisation, and gives an explicit gate-level implementation with error and gate-complexity bounds. Its quantum advantage for observable estimation holds only in sufficiently high spatial dimensions and depends on standard state-preparation and oracle-access assumptions. arXiv:2608.10671 benchmarks HHL and QSVT on FDTD Maxwell systems. It reports infidelities below 2·10⁻³, success probabilities above 10⁻³ and higher accuracy for QSVT. It also finds that the condition number saturates with lattice size, and infers that ill-conditioning should not increase circuit depth.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: The three papers connect the cost of solving a discretized differential equation on a quantum computer to representation or resolution. The third infers circuit-depth implications specifically from conditioning. The brief states that qualification and the oracle assumptions of the second paper.

unannotated_english_cases.question: How model ingredients and evolution stage determine the maximum mass of quark-containing compact stars from TOV solutions
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Model inputs and evolution stage set maximum mass of quark-core stars in three TOV models
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Three model studies link maximum mass to axion/vector terms, early evolution stages, or a stiff hadronic EoS in NJL, Skyrme+MIT, and mPNJL TOV calculations.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are theoretical model calculations, not measurements, of how quark matter equations of state shape the maximum mass of compact stars. The SU(3) NJL study (2608.06024) reports that axion fields and vector interactions significantly influence the EoS and the maximum mass of proto-quark stars at isentropic stages; it also finds that trapped neutrinos raise electron number density and suppress core temperature. The Skyrme plus vector MIT bag study (2608.09195) solves TOV equations for proto-hybrid stars and finds that earlier life stages may play a crucial role in later maximum gravitational mass, for both Maxwell and Gibbs constructions. The modified PNJL study (2608.12653) reports cold hybrid stars above 2 solar masses only if the low-density hadronic EoS is sufficiently stiff, with repulsive vector interactions needed for a stable quark core. The new element is the model-specific attribution of maximum-mass control to each ingredient.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All three calculate a maximum stellar mass using a quark-matter equation of state. The headline calls all objects quark-core stars. The first paper models an entire strange-quark star, while the other two examine hybrid stars.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Resource-theoretic quantification of coherence or entanglement: frameworks for how a quantum or optical resource is measured, structured or transformed
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Three theory papers frame coherence and entanglement as resources via matrices, prisms and channels
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Theory-only preprints give differing frameworks: optical coherence matrices, rank-2 concurrence prisms, and fermionic horizon channel orderings; no experiments reported.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: The three preprints ask how coherence or entanglement is quantified, structured or transformed as a resource, and each gives a different, theoretical answer. arXiv:2608.06356 reviews structured coherence over discrete optical modes with 2x2 and 4x4 coherence matrices, introducing coherence rank, entropy swapping and optical cross-purity, and views coherence as exchangeable, concentrable or spreadable across degrees of freedom. arXiv:2608.07145 extends the concurrence triangle to concurrence prisms for rank-2 three-qubit mixed states and derives a closed-form concurrence fill for GHZ-W mixtures through convex-roof extension. arXiv:2608.08215 derives opposite post-processing orders for exterior and interior fermionic horizon channels, so monotones inherit opposite monotonicity, and numerically illustrates this with QJSD-based coherence in GHS dilaton-black-hole spacetime. These are reviews, derivations and calculations, not laboratory measurements.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: Optical coherence matrices, concurrence of mixed three-qubit states and monotonicity in horizon channels have different physical definitions. The optical tutorial also presents measured coherence ranks and reconstructed images, despite the brief describing the entire set as theory-only.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Symmetry-based seesaw model constructions (flavor, modular or accidental symmetry) that realize neutrino masses and are tied to phenomenology
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Three seesaw constructions use flavor, modular or accidental symmetry to link neutrino masses to testable signals
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Three model-building preprints tie seesaw neutrino masses to leptogenesis, 0νββ or LNV signals via A4, A4 modular or accidental symmetries; none is an experimental measurement.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are theoretical constructions that answer the same question: can a symmetry realize seesaw neutrino masses while linking them to phenomenology? arXiv:2608.06983 proposes Resonant Sequential Dominance, a TBC3 mixing ansatz and an A4×(Z3)^4×(Z2)^2 Lagrangian. It reports consistency with oscillation data and resonant leptogenesis, with a lightest right-handed neutrino mass of 0.13–230 TeV needed for the baryon asymmetry. arXiv:2608.07623 builds all seven two-zero textures in a left-right symmetric model with A4 modular symmetry, using weights 4, 8 and 10 and no flavons. It identifies texture classes that fit neutrino data and baryon asymmetry and give testable effective Majorana masses. arXiv:2608.10062 uses a symmetry-protected texture-zero structure, an accidental symmetry, to allow large lepton-number violation with sub-eV neutrino masses, predicting Heavy Neutral Leptons.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All three construct symmetry-constrained seesaw mass matrices that explain small neutrino masses. The brief attributes the baryon-asymmetry, double-beta-decay and heavy neutral lepton implications to their respective models.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Whether a pulse or phase design for quantum sensing or qubit control achieves its target performance (artifact suppression, frequency-tracking sensitivity, gate fidelity) while remaining robust to control errors
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Pulse designs for qubit sensing and gates: simulated robustness vs a measured silicon-spin fidelity
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Two simulation studies (HSC, ATM) report robust sensing designs; one silicon-spin experiment reports a π/2 gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: The three preprints ask whether a pulse or phase design reaches its performance target while tolerating control errors, but they answer with different evidence. arXiv:2608.06119 proposes a Hadamard-matrix phase design (HSC) for dynamical decoupling sensing; simulations show suppression matching phase randomization, with superior robustness to control errors. arXiv:2608.06636 introduces the adiabatic tangentially-modulated pulse; numerical simulation and analytical modeling show single-shot sensitivity comparable to multi-shot Ramsey averaging and greater robustness to amplitude fluctuations than Shinnar-Le Roux binary-response pulses. arXiv:2608.11072 is the only experimental result: driven silicon spin qubits reach a π/2 gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%, with remaining errors primarily limited by incoherent noise. The sensing results are not experimental demonstrations.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: The sensing papers evaluate artificial spectral responses and frequency-tracking sensitivity. The gate experiment evaluates rotation fidelity. The brief accurately distinguishes the simulations and the experimental fidelity.

Two papers calculate changes to inflationary power spectra beyond slow roll. The third constrains propagation speeds from adiabatic consistency and supplies no corresponding beyond-slow-roll spectrum.

The infrared observations constrain circumstellar composition, the distance estimator evaluates prediction error, and the galaxy comparison measures cloud chemistry. Their source objects or wavelengths provide no common measured outcome.
The three binary studies use timing or spectroscopy for different outputs, respectively secular orbital decay, eccentricity and disk tilt, and a timing search for a third body.
The driven systems supply distinct results on structural phases, magnon energy redistribution and electron transport through impurities. They share no three-paper phase or transport measurement.
The two journal papers form a genuine pair on anharmonic phonon dephasing. The graphene spin texture and cavity-modified solid response do not supply a third determination of that dephasing effect.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Fit of dark-sector or modified-gravity extensions to DESI DR2 late-time expansion data relative to ΛCDM or w0-wa
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Dark-sector and f(Q) fits to DESI DR2: outcomes versus ΛCDM depend on model and data
unannotated_english_cases.summary: In DESI DR2 fits, interacting DE still trails ΛCDM (Bayesian), φ-coupled DM matches w0-wa, and one f(Q) model beats ΛCDM with select SNe sets.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: Three preprints refit published data, including DESI DR2 BAO and supernova compilations, with extensions of ΛCDM. arXiv:2608.21938 combines Planck CMB, DESI DR2, and PantheonPlus, Union3 or DES-Dovekie data. It fits an interacting model with ρ_dm ∝ a^(-3+δ). With constant w, DESI plus supernova data prefer a small negative δ above 2σ. With CPL dark energy, the evidence for interaction weakens and the fit favors quintessence-like evolution. In both cases, Bayesian model comparison favors ΛCDM. arXiv:2608.23712 couples dark matter mass to the dark-energy field (m ∝ φ^α, V ∝ φ^-β) to allow phantom crossing. It implements the model at background and perturbation level, and its best fits match the goodness of fit of w0-wa. arXiv:2608.24676 tests late-time f(Q) gravity with chronometers, DESI DR2, lensing time delays and supernovae. Its square-root exponential model outperforms ΛCDM in χ², AIC and BIC with Pantheon+ or Union 3.0. The power-law model is competitive, but the information criteria do not favor its extra parameter.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All three studies fit cosmological models using DESI DR2 BAO and supernova data. Their baseline and statistic differ. The text distinguishes Bayesian evidence, goodness of fit against evolving dark energy and the supernova-specific gravity comparison.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Degeneracy of the ground space or low-energy states enforced by a symmetry or algebraic structure in a spin Hamiltonian
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Lie-algebraic, anti-unitary and line symmetries fix degeneracies in spin models
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Preprints trace degeneracies to so(3) relations (SO(3) chain), an anti-unitary Z2 (LMG) and line symmetries (chiral XYZ), each in a specific model.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three are theoretical preprints asking how algebraic or symmetry structure enforces ground-space or low-energy degeneracy in spin Hamiltonians; no experiments are reported. arXiv:2608.20849 builds an SO(3)-symmetric nearest-neighbor parent Hamiltonian of an injective MPS assembled from so(3) generators. Under OBC it finds quadratic degeneracy, one irrep per integer spin. Under PBC it finds linear degeneracy, a singlet plus a maximal-spin ferromagnet, with gapless excitations. It attributes this critical behavior to the small parent Hamiltonian, since the 3-site one is gapped and unique. The OBC analysis extends to SO(d) and other compact simple Lie groups. arXiv:2608.21010 shows that, in an anharmonic LMG model, exponentially degenerate doublets survive a parity-breaking term that induces a first-order GSQPT. It traces them to an anti-unitary Z2 inherited from a classical-limit reflection symmetry. arXiv:2608.25224 reports exact, topology-dependent degeneracy from anticommuting noncontractible line symmetries in the chiral XYZ model. Its exact diagonalization up to 9x9 spins gives numerical evidence for a gapless nodal state.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: The three spin models relate Hamiltonian symmetries to degeneracies. The brief distinguishes boundary-dependent multiplicities, exponentially close doublets and exact topology-dependent states, and identifies the numerical gap evidence.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Resource reduction of a compiled or synthesized circuit relative to a baseline, measured as gate count, ancilla count or space-time cost
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Circuit schemes report lower ancilla, upper-bound CNOT and space-time costs vs baselines
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Preprints report fewest ancillas for molecular sparse states, lower model-based CNOT bounds for quantum walks, and ~20–30% space-time savings with √T states.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three preprints construct circuits and report resource savings against a stated baseline. Each uses a different cost metric and reaches a different result. arXiv:2608.20593 compresses sparse molecular wavefunctions, such as those from selected configuration interaction, using GF(2) affine transformations. The Clifford-only stage reduces the dense register to rank r. On its molecular benchmarks, the method uses the fewest ancillary qubits among the evaluated sparse state preparation methods. With optional binary encoding, its non-Clifford gate counts are comparable to those methods. arXiv:2608.25136 decomposes discrete-time quantum walk shift operators on Cayley and torus graphs. It finds lower upper-bound CNOT cost than the naive implementation for k ≤ 64 on inverse-closed graphs and k ≤ 16 on non-inverse-closed graphs. This bound assumes the linear CNOT scaling of Rosa et al. and is largely insensitive to N. arXiv:2608.25797 simulates flag fault-tolerant |√T⟩ preparation on 3D tetrahedral color codes under circuit-level noise. It estimates an approximately 20–30% lower average space-time cost than Clifford+T for synthesizing Haar-random single-qubit unitaries.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: Ancilla count for molecular state preparation, a CNOT bound for a walk shift and space-time cost of single-qubit synthesis refer to different tasks and resources. The individual comparisons and baselines in the text agree with their papers.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Origin of the zero-in-plane-field resistance peak/resistive response in terms of domain-wall spin/valley texture dynamics or domain configuration in graphene valley-polarized states
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Zero-B∥ resistance peak in twisted graphene: wall precession or domain configuration?
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Two twisted-graphene transport studies tie a B∥=0 resistance peak to spin-linked domains; a rhombohedral theory models multicomponent wall precession.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: Two experimental preprints address a sharp longitudinal-resistance peak at zero in-plane field in isospin-ordered twisted graphene. In a twisted graphene heterostructure at fillings with broken isospin degeneracy, arXiv:2608.25257 finds the peak within a fraction of a millitesla of B∥=0. The peak vanishes as current goes to zero. In differential resistance it resolves into resonances that disperse on microtesla and picoampere scales. The authors argue, without establishing it, that current-driven spin-domain-wall precession produces a ferro-Josephson effect. In the valley-polarized quarter metal of twisted double bilayer graphene, arXiv:2608.25263 shows that the metastable peak depends on the orbital-magnetic domain configuration. That configuration is set by the gate-voltage trajectory and by the field, especially B∥, applied during entry. The authors infer that spin, coupled through spin-orbit coupling, is the key degree of freedom but leave the microscopic origin open. A separate theory for rhombohedral graphene, arXiv:2608.26104, finds two domain-wall classes, selected by intervalley Hund's versus spin-orbit coupling. It proposes that precession of the intervalley-coherent phase generates voltage in superconducting junctions and predicts GHz magnetization oscillations, which remain untested.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: The two twisted-graphene experiments measure a resistance peak at zero parallel field. The rhombohedral model predicts voltage across a superconducting junction and GHz oscillations. The text accurately distinguishes the measured peak from this separate prediction.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Choosing between alternative compilations/decompositions/encodings to reduce hardware two-qubit gate cost (CX count, SWAP overhead, depth) for Hamiltonian simulation circuits
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Interaction graph and hardware decide cheapest Hamiltonian-simulation compilation
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Preprints compare fan-out vs sequential, Pauli vs matching, and Bonsai vs JW/BK mappings, finding gains tied to graph degree structure and heavy-hex routing.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: Three preprints ask which compilation, decomposition or encoding minimizes two-qubit cost for Hamiltonian simulation, and each answers differently. The fan-out gadget compiler (2608.20250) is assessed by transpiled resource counts. For the hub-dominated 13-spin case it halves two-qubit depth and cuts volume 1.7-fold, and it lowers gate count on heavy-hex. On all-to-all targets gate count rises for every system, although depth falls up to 2.5-fold. The gain vanishes for dense uniform graphs. In noisy simulations of the tetramethylsilane spectrum, it matches or beats sequential compilation only after post-selection and with error rates 1–1.5 orders of magnitude lower. For CTQWs on all 11,117 connected eight-vertex graphs, 2608.20660 predicts whether Pauli or matching decomposition gives fewer CX gates (MCC 0.569–0.593, driven mainly by n_Pauli). On held-out graphs up to 256 vertices, MCC reaches 1 at N≥64. On seven heavy-hex chips, 2608.25024 finds numerically that routing cancels Bravyi-Kitaev's Pauli-weight advantage, favoring Bonsai. It then runs 2D Hubbard evolution up to 6x6 on hardware.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All three evaluate the entangling-gate or routing cost of alternative Hamiltonian simulation circuits. The brief gives the graph and hardware conditions, reports the noisy comparison as a simulation and separates hardware execution.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Neural surrogates of GS equilibrium/shape used for control or prediction, assessing what the surrogate achieves (accuracy benchmark or control deployment)
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Neural Grad-Shafranov surrogates: numerical benchmark, TCV control test, MAST-U integration
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Surrogates reach 1e-3–1e-2 error vs GS solutions (numerical database); TCV shaping improved without real-time feedback; MAST-U work is integration and testing.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three preprints use neural surrogates of Grad-Shafranov equilibrium or plasma shape for real-time tokamak use, but they report different kinds of evidence. The EXL-50U paper benchmarks MLP, CNN, FNO, Transformer and KAN on a numerical GS database (100,000 IID, 10,000 OOD samples), reporting 1e-3–1e-2 errors relative to GS solutions and a 1e-3 GS-to-device discrepancy; the 0.7 ms TensorRT latency is for CNN. The TCV paper experimentally tests an inverse-GS network mapping a desired boundary to coil currents, reporting improved shaping over standard discharge preparation without explicit real-time shape feedback. Its real-time adaptivity is shown in simulation and only partially in experiment. The MAST-U paper describes a C++ inference server, PCS integration and validation workflow, with no control outcome reported in the abstract.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: The forward surrogate is benchmarked against equilibrium solutions, the inverse surrogate tests shape control on TCV, and the MAST-U report describes deployment and validation. No control or prediction outcome is evaluated by all three. The brief attributes each result accurately.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Sample or query complexity of generating or converting unknown quantum states or unitaries to epsilon accuracy, with scaling in d, r and epsilon
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Sample and query bounds for converting unknown states and unitaries differ by task and in d, r, ε
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Three theory papers give different ε-scaling bounds: block-encoding needs Ω(1/ε) copies, cloning Θ(Mrd/ε), and noisy-unitary purification Θ(d²p/ε) at low noise.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are theoretical and ask how many copies or queries are needed to generate or convert unknown quantum states or unitaries to accuracy ε; none reports an experiment. The answers differ by task. The block-encoding paper (2608.22470) proves Ω(1/ε) state copies for an ε-approximate block-encoding unitary channel, matching known upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. It also proves Ω((1/λmax)√(d/r)) queries to recover a rank-r, d-dimensional state from its block encoding, and derives bounds for ground-state and Gibbs-state preparation. The cloning paper (2608.24484) gives Θ(Mrd/ε) input copies for M clones at worst-case fidelity 1−ε, with a lower bound that already holds for a fixed flat spectrum. The purification paper (2608.26061) gives Θ(d²p/ε) queries for leading-order infidelity ε in the low-noise regime, and the optimal fidelity for noisy unitary conjugation coincides with it to leading order in the low-noise, large-query limit.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: Block encoding, producing additional copies of a state, and purifying a noisy channel have different transformations and error definitions. The individual copy and query bounds are correctly attributed with the low-noise condition for purification.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Tunable design parameter controlling resonance or mode formation in photonic structures (anisotropy, twist, coupling phase)
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Anisotropy, twist and coupling phase proposed as tuning knobs for photonic resonances
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Three preprints each propose a different tuning parameter: SWG anisotropy for BIC waveguides, twist for woodpiles, coupling phase for micro-rings; all are modeled.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: The three preprints share one question: which continuously adjustable design parameter controls resonance or mode formation in a photonic structure. Each gives a different answer. arXiv:2608.20992 proposes artificial anisotropy from subwavelength-grating metamaterials as an independent degree of freedom for reshaping the radiative continuum and forming BIC waveguides. arXiv:2608.22052 reports, from rigorous coupled-wave analysis extended to rotated layers, that woodpile twist angle moves transmission from broadband windows through Fano resonances to a stop band, with a simplified reciprocal-lattice model reproducing the principal resonance changes. arXiv:2608.24523 uses temporal coupled-mode theory to show that phase-controlled super-modes in a lossy-coupled micro-ring system give an absorptive or transparent peak. The abstracts do not report experimental measurements; the results are design proposals or model-based calculations.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: Guided-wave leakage, a twist-dependent transmission band and resonator absorption address different responses. Two full papers actually measure fabricated devices. The brief calls the three contributions model-based designs.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Resource and complexity scaling of quantum differential-equation solvers (circuit count, success probability, time dependence)
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Quantum PDE/ODE solvers: block encoding, tensor networks, Carleman-LCHS cut circuit count, decay, T-dependence
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Three preprints report scaling gains for quantum differential-equation solvers: one circuit per VQLS cost, stabilized success probability, and T-independent complexity.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: The three preprints address resource scaling in quantum solvers for differential equations, but for different equations and bottlenecks. arXiv:2608.19655 reports a VQLS for the Poisson equation using exact block encoding of the discrete Laplacian; it needs one circuit per cost evaluation, versus O(L^2) circuits for LCU-based VQLS. It is benchmarked on three problems and also reports empirically that optimizer choice affects where optimization stalls. arXiv:2608.24150 presents a hybrid tensor-network algorithm for nonlinear terms in quantum CFD; tensor-based block encodings stabilize success probabilities that otherwise decay exponentially with system size, and it reports benchmarks on turbulent flow fields. arXiv:2608.25822 gives a rigorous Carleman-embedding plus LCHS algorithm for weakly nonlinear dissipative ODEs, whose complexity has no explicit dependence on evolution time T, improving on a previous Õ(√T). Its numerical study beyond weak nonlinearity only identifies possible fast-forwarding.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: The Poisson solver counts circuits per cost evaluation, the fluid algorithm studies success probability and the dissipative ODE result removes explicit evolution-time dependence. The summary accurately assigns these distinct bottlenecks.

unannotated_english_cases.question: Whether the proposed Ge hole spin qubit design pairs strong SOC-driven electrical control with reduced charge-noise sensitivity (sweet spots, coherence or quality factor gain)
unannotated_english_cases.headline: Proposed Ge hole qubit designs pair SOC control with charge-noise sweet spots, per models
unannotated_english_cases.summary: Three theory proposals test whether strong spin-orbit control and reduced charge-noise sensitivity coexist in Ge hole qubits; results are model-based, not measured.
unannotated_english_cases.synthesis: All three preprints are theoretical proposals for Ge-based hole spin qubits addressing the same question: whether strong spin-orbit-driven electrical control can coexist with reduced charge-noise sensitivity. The answers differ by design. 2608.21542 models a three-hole Ge/SiGe dot (four-band Luttinger-Kohn–Bir-Pikus) with a p-orbital-encoded qubit, finds charge-noise sweet spots in confinement and magnetic field, and estimates relaxation comparable to single-hole spin qubits. 2608.25852 proposes a Ge-lattice-matched tensile-strained SiGe light-hole qubit with large linear and cubic SOC, a more isotropic spin response, and an improved quality factor versus heavy-hole qubits. 2608.25914 proposes a bilayer Ge/SiGeSn switchable heavy-hole/light-hole qubit; its calculations give a sweet spot with Rabi frequencies near 100 MHz and coherence time near 100 μs, over tenfold longer. None reports an experimental measurement.
unannotated_english_cases.finding: All three Ge qubit designs model electrical driving and decoherence. Two papers locate operating sweet spots. The strained light-hole paper reports a quality factor combining dephasing and drive strength. A common sweet-spot result is too strong.

All three source papers address whether DESI data imply a crossing of the phantom divide. Two quantify the significance at optimal redshifts. The third explicitly interprets BAO trends as crossing and contrasts them with its full-shape inference. They can be compared with those distinctions.
Two papers compare pressures in radio filaments or bubbles. The third estimates deposition of jet energy and the balance against cooling. It supplies no third comparable pressure measurement.

The transistor papers report a voltage window, ion-density control, switching cycles or retained states. The nanofluidic calculation defines memory time as the drive period maximizing the hysteresis area. These are physically different outcomes.

Photoabsorption cross sections and EUV line emission probe atomic spectra. The plasma calculation determines collision frequency and diffusion. No atomic transition or transport coefficient is shared by all three.

The papers respectively address radiation from light-hole excitons, confinement-dependent formation or decay rates and pulsed preparation of quantum-dot exciton states. They do not give three measurements of the same excitation or decay process.

independent_weeks.cost_scope: Dated pilot ledger, cumulative for each restored store. The charge shown per run is the difference from its parent. Failed or unparseable model responses may lack reported use. These retrospective trials do not measure steady-state monthly operating expense.

public_english_check.method: Checked HTML language and canonical URLs for public field entry points, sitemap, indexed language, Atom language, old redirects, and editorial text fields in dated rankings and topic histories for Hangul. Source titles and credited author names retain their published form.
